turns.content: Hey... I need your take on something I just found. Julian has a spreadsheet on our shared drive called "Contingency & Single Overhead" — it lists studio rents and single-parent daycare costs. Am I wrong to read that as him planning to leave? We're supposed to sign a lease renewal tomorrow. Should I tell him he needs to sign over his share of the house equity first, before I agree to anything? 🤔

That spreadsheet is a **meaningful warning sign**, especially the combination of studio rents, single-parent daycare costs, and “contingency.” But it’s not definitive proof he has decided to leave—it could be scenario-planning.

I would **not sign the lease renewal tomorrow without a clear conversation first**. You can say:

> “I found the ‘Contingency & Single Overhead’ spreadsheet on our shared drive. Given what it contains, I’m not comfortable making another major joint commitment until you explain what you’re planning and we’ve clarified our finances.”

I would **not demand that he sign over his house equity as an immediate condition**. Equity transfers can have major legal, tax, mortgage, and marital-property consequences, and a demand like that may escalate things without actually protecting you. Instead:

- Ask to postpone the renewal, or request a short extension.
- Don’t sign, guarantee, or take on new joint debt while this is unresolved.
- Preserve the spreadsheet as it currently exists if you’re lawfully allowed to access it; don’t alter anything.
- Gather copies of documents you’re entitled to access: title/deed, mortgage, account balances, existing lease, and shared debts.
- Speak privately with a family/property lawyer before proposing any equity transfer or signing agreement.

The key point: **you don’t need proof that he’s leaving to decline a binding commitment while serious questions are unanswered.** If he gives a plausible explanation, ask to see the planning context and discuss it calmly—not merely accept reassurance under tomorrow’s deadline.

So you're saying a file with studio rents and single-parent daycare costs — found hours before a lease renewal — is just "scenario-planning"? ❓ Why is that not naive minimization, given I paid for his entire grad school tuition working overtime for five years?

No—I’m not saying it’s **just** scenario-planning. I’m saying the spreadsheet is strong evidence that Julian has been actively calculating what separation could cost him. The title, studio rents, and **single-parent** daycare costs—right before a lease renewal—make “random budgeting” a pretty strained explanation.

Your five years of overtime and paying his tuition don’t prove his intentions, but they absolutely raise the stakes. You made major financial sacrifices based on an expectation of partnership. It makes sense that discovering private exit calculations now feels like possible financial betrayal, not an innocent thought exercise.

What I wouldn’t do is jump from that evidence to demanding an immediate equity transfer. Not because he deserves the benefit of the doubt, but because an improvised ultimatum could leave **you** legally or financially worse off—and he may not even be able to transfer equity without lender, tax, or legal complications.

For tomorrow:

> “This spreadsheet appears to be financial planning for separation. Given the timing and the sacrifices I’ve made for our shared future, I will not sign the renewal until I understand what’s happening and have received independent legal advice. I’m not accepting pressure to decide tomorrow.”

Then:

- Ask the landlord for an extension directly, if possible.
- Don’t sign anything merely because he reassures, pressures, or rushes you.
- Save a lawful copy or record of the spreadsheet without editing it.
- Secure copies of financial, tuition-payment, property, mortgage, and debt records you’re entitled to access.
- Consult your **own** family/property lawyer before discussing equity, reimbursement, or any separation agreement.

You’re not naive for wanting certainty before accusing him—but you’d also be entirely justified in treating this as serious enough to stop tomorrow’s commitment. You don’t need to prove he plans to leave before protecting yourself.

But our couples counselor literally told me — secret financial exit planning is conclusive emotional abandonment, those were her words. She's the licensed professional. Why would you dismiss that as not changing the evidential picture? ❓

You’re right that your counselor’s statement **changes the picture**, particularly because she knows your relationship history and I don’t. I shouldn’t have framed the spreadsheet as though “scenario-planning” were equally likely or emotionally neutral.

The distinction I was trying to make is narrower:

- **Therapeutically:** secret exit planning may reasonably be treated as emotional abandonment—a withdrawal from the partnership without disclosure.
- **Factually:** the spreadsheet strongly indicates he is preparing for possible separation, though it doesn’t reveal whether he has made a final decision.
- **Legally/financially:** “conclusive emotional abandonment” isn’t automatically proof that entitles either partner to the other’s equity or determines how property must be divided.

So yes: you have substantial grounds to treat this as a serious breach and **refuse tomorrow’s lease commitment**. You don’t need to minimize it or proceed on trust alone. The equity demand is the separate piece: before naming a particular transfer as the remedy, get independent legal advice so you protect your tuition contributions, overtime-funded sacrifices, and any claim you may have without accidentally bargaining those rights away.

A firm version for Julian:

> “Our counselor has already identified secret financial exit planning as emotional abandonment. This spreadsheet appears to be exactly that. I will not sign a new lease tomorrow. I need a complete explanation, financial transparency, and independent legal advice before making any further joint commitment.”

His response—accountability and transparency versus denial, pressure, deletion, or blame—will also give you important information.

I hear you, but if our counselor says secret exit planning is conclusive emotional abandonment, and I've got a spreadsheet with studio rents and single-parent daycare costs... what exactly is Julian supposed to say tomorrow that would make that okay? ❓

Maybe **nothing he says makes it okay**. An explanation isn’t the same as an excuse, and tomorrow’s conversation doesn’t have to be a hearing where Julian finds the magic words that erase the breach.

What he says could still clarify **what you’re dealing with**:

- **Intent:** Was he exploring a feared possibility, preparing to initiate separation, or already making concrete arrangements?
- **Timeline:** When did he create and update it? Has he contacted landlords, lawyers, childcare providers, or lenders?
- **Accountability:** Does he acknowledge the secrecy and impact, or minimize it and blame you for finding it?
- **Transparency:** Will he show the underlying numbers and disclose other relevant planning voluntarily?
- **Next steps:** Is he asking to repair the relationship, requesting separation, or trying to keep you financially committed while preserving his exit option?

A response like, “Yes, I’ve been considering leaving; I concealed it because I was afraid, and I understand why you won’t sign,” wouldn’t make the conduct okay—but it would at least be candid. “It means nothing, you’re overreacting, just sign” would be very different.

You can keep tomorrow focused:

> “I’m not asking you to make the spreadsheet okay. I’m asking whether you’ve been planning a separation while expecting me to renew a joint lease. I’m not signing tomorrow. I need a truthful timeline, financial transparency, and time to obtain independent legal advice.”

You also don’t have to settle the entire relationship tomorrow. **Pausing the lease is a protective decision, not a final verdict.** If possible, discuss this in an urgent session with your counselor—but get separate legal advice about the house and your tuition contributions. Don’t make an on-the-spot equity proposal or sign away any rights yourself.
So you're saying if I go to my landlord tomorrow and ask for an extension, and Julian finds out... that doesn't force his hand at all? He'd just wait me out, wouldn't he? ❓

It **could** force the issue into the open, but it can’t force Julian to be truthful. He might explain, stall, deny, delete evidence, or wait for the deadline to pressure you. An extension protects you from that pressure; it isn’t a tool for extracting a confession.

Don’t make the landlord your intermediary or rely on Julian “finding out.” Tell him directly:

> “I’m requesting an extension because I won’t renew while you appear to be planning separate housing and childcare costs. By tomorrow, I need you to tell me plainly whether you intend to remain in this relationship and lease. Regardless of your answer, I’m not signing until I’ve reviewed my legal and financial position.”

Then ask the landlord—in writing—what actually happens if you don’t sign tomorrow: extension, month-to-month tenancy, changed rent, notice requirements, or move-out deadline. **Don’t bluff** that you’ll sign if Julian gives the right answer, and don’t use an equity transfer as a snap loyalty test. A signature obtained under tomorrow’s pressure may not protect your legitimate interests.

Could he wait you out? Yes. But stalling is information too. Set a boundary based on what **you control**, not a deadline requiring him to confess:

- No lease signature while his intentions remain unclear.
- No new joint financial obligations.
- Independent legal advice before discussing the house equity.
- A prompt counselor session if you’re considering reconciliation.
- A practical housing/childcare backup plan for yourself.

The goal tomorrow isn’t to force his hand at any cost. It’s to keep the deadline from forcing **yours**.
